This review qualitatively examines the literature on the use of SAR in elderly care and aims to establish the roles this technology may play in the future. DESIGN: Scoping review. DATA SOURCES: Search of CINAHL, Cochrane Library, Embase, MEDLINE, PsychINFO and Scopus databases was conducted, complemented with a free search using Google Scholar and reference harvesting. The main search was conducted in March 2016, and the latest search was conducted in September 2017. ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA: The inclusion criteria consist of elderly participants, any elderly healthcare facility, humanoid and pet robots and all social interaction types with the robot. Exclusions were acceptability studies, technical reports of robots and publications surrounding physically or surgically assistive robots. RESULTS: In total, 61 final publications were included in the review, describing 33 studies and including 1574 participants and 11 robots. 28 of the 33 papers report positive findings. Five roles of SAR were identified: affective therapy, cognitive training, social facilitator, companionship and physiological therapy. CONCLUSIONS: Although many positive outcomes were reported, a large proportion of the studies have methodological issues, which limit the utility of the results. Nonetheless, the reported value of SAR in elderly care does warrant further investigation. Future studies should endeavour to validate the roles demonstrated in this review. # Social robots used with older people: a map of the evidence

This map covers studies where a robot was deployed with older people. I left out most attitude and acceptance surveys, design papers, and ethics papers, with a few exceptions noted below. I read abstracts rather than full texts, and I ran about ten searches, so this is a map and not an exhaustive review. I did not search for individual platforms such as Pepper, Zora, Kompaï, Care-O-bot or Ryan. A targeted search for Pepper returned almost no Pepper-with-older-adults studies, so that is a gap to check.

## 1. Which robots, and with whom

| Robot type | Examples | Typical participants and settings |
|---|---|---|
| **Pet or animal-like robots** | PARO seal, AIBO dog, robotic cats | People with dementia, or older people with depression. Nursing homes, long-term care, dementia day care, and some home use |
| **Humanoid robots** | NAO | Residents with dementia, and residential-care residents in theatre-based mood interventions |
| **Companion or service robots** | MARIO, Hobbit | MARIO: people with dementia in residential care. Hobbit: community-dwelling older adults in their own homes |
| **Exercise or coaching robots** | Fasola & Matarić's robot exercise coach | Older adults doing seated exercise |
| **Telepresence robots** | GIRAFF/ROBIN | Older adults living at home |
| **Conversational robots** | "Sunshine" chat robot; a conversational robot for Alzheimer's cognitive assessment | Older adults with cognitive impairment |

PARO is by far the best-studied platform. The same research groups, such as Moyle and colleagues in Australia, appear repeatedly.

## 2. Findings by robot and setting

### A. PARO in nursing homes and long-term care (most mature evidence)
- **Cognitively impaired residents, mixed outcomes.** A pilot randomized crossover trial of 18 residents with mid- to late-stage dementia found a moderate-to-large positive effect of PARO on quality of life, and higher pleasure scores, compared with a reading group [W1488883230]. The authors called for larger trials.
- **Sleep.** A cluster RCT in 10 Norwegian nursing homes (60 residents with dementia) ran 30-minute PARO group sessions twice a week for 12 weeks. It found better sleep efficiency, longer total sleep time, and fewer night awakenings than treatment as usual [W3088196398].
- **Depression, loneliness and quality of life.** A Taiwanese study of 20 older adults with depression in long-term care gave each person a PARO to keep for 8 weeks. Depression and loneliness fell and quality of life rose [W3015603533]. This was a single-group before-and-after design, so it is weaker evidence than an RCT.
- **Individual variation.** Reflections on a cluster RCT (PARO vs. plush toy vs. usual care) found considerable variation in how residents responded, and raised ethical questions about giving and retrieving the robot [W2778691880].
- **Observational and qualitative work.** Studies cover group sensory therapy in nursing homes [W2040979576, W4243437205], a three-month naturalistic field study with PARO in a public area [W2039822570], and the social shaping of PARO by staff, residents and visitors [W2043587319]. Others look at verbal and emotional responses by dementia severity [W1505024467] and at how people with dementia perceive PARO in relation to pain and mood [W2985514812]. A pilot RCT on chronic pain was reported as a conference abstract [W3097289914].

### B. PARO in community and home settings
A pilot block RCT with 30 dyads at two dementia day care centres and in participants' homes in New Zealand ran for 12 weeks [W2732925385]. PARO significantly improved facial expressions (affect) and communication with staff. There were no significant differences in dementia symptoms or physiological measures. People with less cognitive impairment responded better.

### C. Comparing robot types
- **NAO vs. PARO vs. real dog.** A study in a Spanish nursing home and day care centre (101 and 110 residents in two phases, plus 20 and 17 day-care patients) ran sessions twice a week for 3 months [W1807810766].
  - Robot groups improved on apathy.
  - The NAO group's MMSE score declined, but its sMMSE score did not.
  - QUALID scores rose in the PARO group.
  - In day care, NAO was associated with improved irritability and total NPI.
  - Several comparisons showed no difference between groups.
- **AIBO vs. living dog.** A robotic dog and a living dog both reduced loneliness in long-term care residents compared with no animal-assisted therapy. Residents became attached to both [W2132164645].
- **AIBO in dementia.** Visits with a live dog and with AIBO both stimulated social interaction beyond a visitor alone. AIBO prompted longer looks and more resident-initiated conversation than the dog [W1972564462].

### D. Companion robots for dementia (MARIO)
In a 4-week pilot with 10 people with dementia in an Irish nursing home, participants stayed interested in MARIO and accepted it, and they spent more time socially engaged. Quality of life, depression and perceived social support did not change significantly [W2955051104]. The sample was small and the period short. Related MARIO work covers loneliness [W2889731820] and stakeholder perceptions [W3105249390].

### E. Robots in people's own homes
- **Hobbit.** In 16 private households (aged 75+), all users interacted with the robot daily over several weeks. They rated most functions as working well, and the robot's adaptive behaviour made interaction easier over time. Non-scripted interaction exposed real-world problems, such as misinterpreted actions [W2994761079]. An earlier HRI paper reports first results from 18 households [W3137166629].
- **Companion robot field test.** Eight seniors living alone used a robot for about 95 days. They accepted it enthusiastically. Navigation and speech recognition were the most useful functions but also the least reliable [W2717439789].
- **Telepresence.** Long-term evaluations of GIRAFF/ROBIN at home are in [W2259814160, W2743226003, W2394797369].
- **Robot companion cats at home** for people with dementia were studied in a qualitative case study [W3034490183].
- **Sensing SARs** were studied in the homes of older adults with depression [W2953482672].

### F. Other uses: exercise, physical therapy, cognition, community
- **Exercise coaching.** Two user studies found a strong preference for a relational (praising, personalized) robot coach over a non-relational one. The system was rated highly across metrics [W2065178260; see also W1967507142].
- **Physical therapy for dementia.** A long-term autonomous robot accompanied two weekly walking groups for a month. Therapists saw potential gains in motivation, group cohesion and mood. Technical unreliability turned the robot into extra workload for therapists [W4251569456].
- **Social connectedness.** One study examined a robot facilitating human-to-human engagement in an assisted-living community [W2943699887].
- **Theatre and NAO.** Creative-arts and NAO interventions aimed to improve mood in residential care [W2982896790, W2899915867].
- **Longitudinal ethics study.** Retirement-village residents had eight sessions over 4 weeks with a robot that showed either emotive or non-emotive behaviour. Emotive behaviour did not change acceptance or attachment. Attachment stayed low to medium, and perceived ease of use rose over time [W3001702224].
- **Other pilots:**
  - A memory game with a socially assistive robot in a long-term care facility [W2003566851].
  - A social robot collecting patient-reported outcome measures from older patients [W2946005838].
  - A conversational robot for older adults with Alzheimer's [W3033476063].
  - A "Sunshine" chat robot during COVID-19 [W3041860695].

## 3. What the reviews conclude
- **Meta-analysis of RCTs** [W2808281222]. It found 13 articles from 11 RCTs, with 9 in the meta-analysis.
  - Pooled effects on agitation, anxiety and quality of life were positive but not statistically significant.
  - The narrative synthesis suggested better engagement, interaction and stress indicators, and less loneliness and medication use.
  - Risk of bias was high, notably for allocation concealment and blinding.
- **Scoping review** [W2789445850]. It covered 33 studies, 1,574 participants and 11 robots, and 28 of 33 reported positive findings. It identified five roles: affective therapy, cognitive training, social facilitator, companionship, and physiological therapy. Many studies had methodological problems.
- **Animal-assisted interventions with dogs or robot animals in dementia** [W2946010724]. Of the included articles, 6 of 11 showed reduced behavioural and psychological symptoms, 6 of 9 showed less depression or better mood, and 3 of 5 showed better quality of life.
- **Other reviews to read:**
  - Depression [W2889960145].
  - Aging and dementia [W2888482633].
  - Qualitative experience of older adults [W2586081748].
  - In-home robotics [W3004202241].
  - Telepresence in dementia [W2751864896].
  - Barriers and enablers for humanoids [W2999297198].
  - Earlier reviews [W2000476293, W2045063968].

## 4. Cross-cutting patterns and gaps
1. **The evidence is concentrated.** Most of it is PARO, in dementia, in institutional settings. Evidence for cognitively healthy community-dwelling older people is thinner and mostly feasibility or acceptance work (Hobbit, the companion robot field test).
2. **Effects are modest and inconsistent.** Affect, engagement, social interaction and sleep show the most consistent signals. Dementia symptoms, quality of life, and depression results are mixed. Several trials found no significant differences on standardized scales even when engagement was good [W2732925385, W2955051104, W1807810766].
3. **Responses differ between people.** Cognitive impairment level moderated the response in several studies [W2732925385, W1505024467], and individual variation is stressed in [W2778691880].
4. **Study quality is limited.** Reviews and the primary studies themselves note small samples, short follow-up, and weak blinding. There are few large RCTs.
5. **Reliability and deployment issues.** Home and therapy-support deployments repeatedly report technical problems (navigation, speech recognition, robustness). These can burden staff [W4251569456, W2717439789, W2994761079].
6. **Ethics.** Deception, attachment, and removing the robot at the end of a study come up in [W2778691880, W3001702224].

# Social robots with people living with dementia

I narrowed the earlier list to studies where the participants were people with dementia, and I added what I'd missed.

- I included a study only if its abstract said dementia (or Alzheimer's) was the population. Where dementia was mixed with other groups, I flagged it.
- I read abstracts only, not full texts.
- The tool-call limit hit before I could check three records: W1178530349 (robotic pets for dementia residents), W2900350517 (a socially assistive robot for apathy) and W2982896790 (NAO with theatre). Only the first looks likely to be relevant, so check these before relying on this list.

## 1. Controlled and comparative studies in care homes

| Study | Robot and comparison | Participants and setting | Findings |
|---|---|---|---|
| [W1488883230] | PARO vs. reading group (randomized crossover) | 18 residents with mid-to-late-stage dementia, one Australian aged care facility | Moderate-to-large positive effect on quality of life and higher pleasure scores. The authors say a larger trial is needed. |
| [W3088196398] (thesis: [W3102212853]) | PARO group activity vs. treatment as usual (cluster RCT) | 60 residents with dementia, special care units in 10 Norwegian nursing homes, twice a week for 12 weeks | Better sleep efficiency and total sleep time, fewer night awakenings. The thesis also examined agitation, depression, psychotropic use and quality of life, but its abstract reports no results. |
| [W2778691880] | PARO vs. plush toy vs. usual care (cluster RCT) | Long-term care residents with dementia | This paper is a qualitative reflection on five participants. It reports wide variation in individual responses and ethical issues around giving and retrieving PARO. The trial's quantitative results are reported elsewhere. |
| [W2894885829] | PARO vs. control (quasi-experimental) | 33 nursing home residents with dementia in Korea, 12 sessions | Significant differences in positive emotions and problem behaviours between groups. The PARO group improved significantly on social interaction. |
| [W1807810766] | NAO, PARO and a real dog vs. control | 101 and 110 nursing home residents in two phases, plus 20 and 17 day-care patients, twice a week for 3 months | Apathy improved in the robot groups. The NAO group's MMSE score declined, but its sMMSE score did not. QUALID scores rose in the PARO group. Day-care NAO use was linked to better irritability and NPI total score. Several comparisons showed no difference. |
| [W2294211165] | PARO vs. dog vs. toy cat (randomized) | 100 nursing home residents, 12 visits each | Participants varied in cognitive impairment, so this is not strictly dementia-only. The dog and PARO drew the most physical contact, eye contact and speech. The more impaired the resident, the more interaction was directed to the animal. PARO did not hold attention over time. |
| [W1505024467] | PARO vs. stuffed lion | 19 residents with mild/moderate and 11 with severe dementia | Both groups talked more to PARO, showed more positive emotional change, and laughed more. Staff communication with mild/moderate residents was higher with the lion. |
| [W2074069593] | Robotic cat vs. plush cat | Dementia special care unit in a nursing home | Similar trends for both cats: less agitation and more pleasure and interest. |
| [W1972564462] | AIBO vs. live dog vs. visitor alone | Female nursing home residents with dementia | The dog and AIBO each stimulated more social interaction than the visitor alone. AIBO prompted longer looks and more resident-initiated conversation than the dog. |
| [W4407738599] | PARO vs. stuffed animal in occupational therapy | Patients with dementia | The authors conclude robot therapy differs from therapy with inanimate objects and can encourage patients to be more self-directive. |
| [W2985514812] (trial abstract: [W3097289914]) | PARO, 30 minutes, 5 days a week for 6 weeks | Residents with mild-to-moderate dementia and chronic pain, three aged care facilities | In interviews (n=11), residents reported mood improvement and relaxation for pain relief. They also noted limits of PARO's weight and voice, and their responses fluctuated. The pilot RCT's outcome data are not in what I retrieved. |

## 2. Observational and small studies of PARO group sessions
- Eight-week group sensory therapy in a nursing home, with participants at varying cognitive impairment levels [W4243437205].
- A related report on 10 residents with varying dementia, covering interaction modalities [W2040979576].

## 3. Community settings (day care and home)
- **RCT, Auckland** [W2732925385]. 30 dyads in two day care centres and at home, over 12 weeks.
  - PARO significantly improved facial expressions and communication with staff at day care.
  - There were no significant differences in dementia symptoms or physiological measures.
  - People with less cognitive impairment responded better.
  - The thesis version [W2995685337] reports 28 dyads and adds that caregiver burden, stress and quality of life showed limited effects. The two sources differ on sample size, so check this.
- **Single-session PARO study** [W2080233792]. 11 community-dwelling people with mild cognitive impairment or mild-to-moderate dementia (this is a mixed group). Most stayed focused for the whole session. Mood scores improved but not significantly. Inter-rater reliability of the observation method was good.
- **AIBO, early dementia** [W2159536297]. 24 older people with small cognitive deficits (MMSE>23). Acceptability looked promising, especially for those comfortable with technology. This is a preliminary conference paper.

## 4. Robots in people's homes or supported living
- **Matilda (Australia).** Deployed in several households for six months. Authors report sensory enrichment, social connectivity, and respite for partners [W1994379356]. This is a service-architecture paper, so evidence is limited.
- **Betty (home care).** A longitudinal study found that older people with dementia engaged with the robot at home. The authors argue for personalizing services around personhood [W2944083468].
- **Robot cat.** A qualitative case study of people with dementia at home and their families found distraction, communication and mood effects where the cat was accepted, and rejection in some cases [W3034490183].
- **Companion animals.** Two qualitative studies, one comparing a live dog with a robot in a care home and one a longitudinal case of a person with Alzheimer's bonding with a robotic pet, suggest benefit for social and emotional life [W3198896322].
- **Joy for All robot animals.** Six-month diary data from two supported living sites for people with dementia or learning difficulties (a mixed group). Use rose and settled into near-permanent availability. Reported outcomes were reminiscence, better communication, and possibly less agitation or anxiety. Some people found the robots "creepy" [W3015009700].

## 5. MARIO and other non-pet robots
- **MARIO quantitative pilot.** 10 people with dementia in an Irish nursing home, up to 12 sessions over 4 weeks. Sustained interest and acceptance, and more time socially engaged. No significant change in quality of life, depression or perceived social support [W2955051104].
- **MARIO multiple case study.** MARIO supported resilience in 8 of 10 people, but people with dementia needed skilled facilitation to use it [W3092218325].
- **MARIO qualitative studies.** Interviews across the UK, Italy and Ireland (38 people with dementia, plus relatives, carers and managers) were mostly positive. Voice recognition was a problem, and some staff worried robots might replace them [W3105249390]. The Irish loneliness pilot is [W2889731820].
- **Sophie and Jack (Australia).** Over 11,000 behavioural reactions from 139 people with dementia over 5 years were coded. Authors report sensory enrichment, positive social engagement and entertainment [W2317990020]. Matilda was trialed with 115 participants in residential care, with significant improvements in emotional, visual and behavioural engagement [W2564685734]. Both are observational and mostly come from one group.
- **Walking group.** A long-term autonomous robot accompanied two weekly walking groups for older adults with advanced dementia. Therapists saw potential gains in motivation, group cohesion and mood. Technical failures turned it into extra workload [W4251569456].
- **Conversational robot.** In a pilot with people with Alzheimer's, conversations were better with humans, but participants generally liked the robot, and it held their interest [W3033476063].

## 6. Reviews specific to dementia
- Dogs and robotic animals in nursing homes. Of the included articles, 6 of 11 showed fewer behavioural and psychological symptoms, 6 of 9 less depression or better mood, and 3 of 5 better quality of life [W2946010724].
- Social robots in aging and dementia [W2888482633].
- Telepresence robots for connectedness in dementia [W2751864896].
- A dementia care overview [W2060479977].

## 7. Patterns in the dementia evidence
1. **PARO dominates.** Care-home and day-care settings dominate. Home-based evidence is mostly qualitative, case-based, or from one group.
2. **Engagement and affect are the most consistent findings.** Positive emotion, social interaction, and sleep show the clearest signals. Standardized symptom and quality-of-life scales often show nothing significant [W2732925385, W2955051104].
3. **Severity moderates response.** Findings differ by dementia severity. In several studies, people with less impairment responded better [W2732925385, W2995685337]. In others, more impaired people directed more interaction to the animal [W2294211165].
4. **Facilitation matters.** Several studies describe staff or facilitator mediation as important [W3092218325, W2039822570 is related but not dementia-specific].
5. **Novelty may fade for PARO** [W2294211165], while the Joy for All diaries suggest sustained use [W3015009700].
6. **Control comparisons are mixed.** Plush toys often produced similar trends [W2074069593, W1505024467].

## 8. Excluded or uncertain
Dropped because participants were not dementia-specific:
- PARO naturalistic nursing home studies [W2039822570, W2043587319]
- Taiwan PARO study (depression) [W3015603533]
- AIBO and loneliness [W2132164645]
- Multicentre Japanese nursing home study [W2898061611]
- Multi-robot aged care trial [W1945345301]
- Robot-assisted therapy in institutionalized older adults [W1510372641]
- Brian 2.1 memory game in long-term care [W2003566851, W2024647503]
- Exercise, telepresence, Hobbit and home companion field tests

Not verified or not usable:
- "Sunshine" chat robot [W3041860695] was a letter in which the abstract says only "cognitive impairment".
- The robot music therapist [W759765632] has no participant detail in its abstract.
- A protocol for humanoid robot vs. tablet training in home care for dementia [W2975531399] has no results.
- A health-care provider interview study about PARO [W2689483015] has no people with dementia as participants.
- An infection-control study of companion robots in care homes [W3081435517] is a practical read, not a dementia-specific one.

A telepresence robot carries a remote person's video and voice. It isn't itself the social partner. I listed these in the first map without flagging that.

- **Hobbit** [W2994761079, W3137166629] is described as an "assistive, social service robot". Its field trials emphasised manipulation, autonomous navigation and everyday-task help alongside interaction. It is a mix of physical assistance and social interaction.

- **Exercise coaching robots** [W2065178260, W1967507142] are socially assistive robots that motivate exercise. They don't physically move the person's body. - **The walking-group robot for people with advanced dementia** [W4251569456] supports physical therapy. It offers visual and acoustic stimulation and group motivation and doesn't physically assist.
